note: 🧭️ Node-by-node keyboard traversal of the flow node graph, stated once and answered twice. `graph` is a language-neutral restatement of the bundled `hexagonal-mushroom-column` example — the Rust law asserts it is EQUAL to that example's own widgets/layout/synapses, so the fixture can never drift from the document a user actually opens. `keyboardOrder` is the reading order the traversal walks: ascending layout x, then ascending layout y, then the document's own widget order. `walks` are arrow sequences: each step names one `FlowGraphStep` and the selection ids it must leave behind; a step with nowhere to go leaves the selection UNCHANGED and is written as the repeated row (a source node has nothing upstream of it). `anchors` states how a non-node selection is reduced to the node a step starts from — a port handle (`{node}@{port}`, what `activateSelection` selects) steps from its owning node, so arrowing after opening a node closes it again. The Rust half answers this through `FlowFixture::keyboard_step` and the app's own reducer; the TypeScript twin re-implements the traversal from this file alone and must reach the same ids. Driven by `✏️editor/🎮️commands/🧭️navigate-graph/🧪️tests/🔬️unit/🦀️.rs` and `🧪️tests/🔬️unit/🟦️.ts`; this file, not either of them, is the statement.

anchors.why: Nothing selected: a forward step enters at the first node, a backward step at the last.
One node selected is the anchor.
A port handle steps from the node that owns it.
A multi-selection steps from its FIRST member in reading order, never from whichever id the set happened to hold first.
An id the document no longer holds is no anchor at all; the step re-enters the graph rather than refusing.

walks.name: arrow-down walks the whole reading order and wraps
arrow-up enters at the last node and walks back
arrow-right follows the wires to the preview and then holds
arrow-left follows the wires back to a source and then holds
a fork upstream takes the first candidate in reading order, not in wire order
walking from an opened node's port closes it back onto a node
